title: What a computer is: CPU, RAM, disk, and why the difference matters
story:
Start with the idea that made the question possible. John von Neumann circulated the First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC from the Moore School of Electrical Engineering at the University of Pennsylvania on 30 June 1945, describing a machine that holds both its instructions and its data in the same addressable memory, from which a control unit fetches and decodes them in sequence. The contrast is ENIAC, built at the same school, which was programmed by setting switches and plugging cable connections between its units — so changing the computation was a rewiring job, not a loading job.

Putting instructions in memory is what makes software possible. It also means that everything a processor does, including deciding what to do next, is a memory access — which is why the speed of memory, rather than the speed of arithmetic, is the thing that ends up mattering.

Here is the shape of it, from the latency table compiled by Jeff Dean, originally by Peter Norvig. An L1 cache reference is 0.5 ns. A branch mispredict is 5 ns, an L2 cache reference 7 ns, a mutex lock and unlock 25 ns. A main memory reference is 100 ns — which the table itself labels 200x L1, and that multiplier is the whole lesson. Reading 4K randomly from a solid-state drive is 150,000 ns. A round trip within the same datacenter is 500,000 ns. A disk seek is 10,000,000 ns, or 20x a datacenter round trip. Reading 1 MB sequentially from disk is 20,000,000 ns, and sending a packet from California to the Netherlands and back is 150,000,000 ns.

Those gaps are hard to feel, so scale them. If an L1 reference took one second of human time, main memory would take a minute and three quarters — walking down the hall. A random solid-state read would take a day and three quarters. A round trip inside the same datacenter would take nearly six days. A disk seek would take about four months. And the packet to the Netherlands and back would take nearly five years.

Read that ordering again, because the ranking is the part that changes how you write code: a round trip to another machine in the same building is roughly twenty times cheaper than moving a disk head. Talking to a computer across the room beats waiting for a spinning platter, which is why so much of systems design consists of arranging never to touch the slowest thing.

One caution that matters more than any individual figure. The table's values date from around 2012 and drift with each hardware generation — later revisions give register access about 0.3 ns, L1 about 1 ns, L2 about 4 ns, L3 about 15 ns and main memory about 80 ns, and readers note that current solid-state drives are faster than the listed number. So quoting the figures as current is a mistake. The durable content is the ratios: cache is about two orders of magnitude faster than main memory, memory about three orders faster than a solid-state drive, and anything crossing a building or a continent is in its own category entirely.

problem.name: The memory hierarchy
problem.shape: Code has to reach data, and where the data lives changes the cost by orders of magnitude.
tell: a loop is slow and its arithmetic is trivial
performance changes when the data grows past a size rather than a count
a function is called in a loop and reaches a different machine each time
a design treats memory and disk as interchangeable with different capacities
problem.move: For any hot operation, identify which level of the hierarchy it touches and how many times. Count the crossings rather than the instructions, since one avoided disk seek is worth tens of millions of cache references, and prefer sequential access at every level because it is the access pattern each level is built for.
problem.invariant: Each level down the hierarchy is orders of magnitude slower than the one above. The count of crossings dominates the cost of the work done between them.
problem.breaks: The absolute figures go stale with each hardware generation — the widely quoted table is from around 2012, and later revisions move nearly every line. Quoting it as current is wrong, and the ordering can invert: a fast local solid-state read can now beat a slow cross-datacenter round trip, so the hierarchy has to be re-derived for the hardware in front of you.

cost.time: reasoning about layout and access patterns rather than about algorithms, which is less portable knowledge and dates with the hardware
cost.space: the usual remedy is to keep a copy nearer the processor, which costs memory and creates a second thing that can be stale
cost.beats: treating all storage as uniform, which is simpler and wrong by orders of magnitude, and optimising instruction counts, which improves the part that was not the cost

worked.problem: Explain the latency numbers every engineer is expected to know, and what they dictate about indexing and caching.
worked.reasoning:
The numbers are worth knowing as ratios rather than as values, and the ratios are large enough that they decide designs on their own.

Working down the table compiled by Jeff Dean, originally by Peter Norvig: an L1 cache reference is 0.5 ns. A branch mispredict is 5 ns, an L2 reference 7 ns, a mutex lock and unlock 25 ns. A main memory reference is 100 ns, labelled in the table as 200x L1. Reading 4K randomly from a solid-state drive is 150,000 ns. A round trip inside the same datacenter is 500,000 ns. A disk seek is 10,000,000 ns, noted as 20x a datacenter round trip. Reading 1 MB sequentially from disk is 20,000,000 ns, and California to the Netherlands and back is 150,000,000 ns.

Scale them to human time at one second per nanosecond, because that is what makes them usable. L1 is a second. Main memory is a minute and three quarters. A random solid-state read is a day and three quarters. A datacenter round trip is nearly six days. A disk seek is about four months. The intercontinental packet is nearly five years.

The ordering is the surprising part and it is the part that changes code. A round trip to a different machine in the same building is roughly twenty times cheaper than moving a disk head. Talking to another computer beats waiting for a platter.

Which is exactly why an index exists. Without one, answering a query means reading the table, and a large table means many seeks — each one four human months. An index turns that into a small number of seeks by making the search structure shallow, so the entire purpose of the data structure is reducing the count of crossings into the slowest level. The same logic explains why an index that does not fit in memory behaves so differently from one that does: the lookups themselves start crossing, and the structure that was supposed to save seeks begins causing them.

Caching is the same argument applied one level up. Keeping a result nearer the processor converts a crossing into a reference, and because the ratio is orders of magnitude, a modest hit rate pays for itself immediately — which is why caches appear at every level of every real system, and why the interesting engineering is never whether to cache but how to know when the copy is wrong.

And this is where the honest caveat belongs, because these numbers are quoted with more confidence than they deserve. The table dates from around 2012 and drifts with hardware. Later revisions give register access about 0.3 ns, L1 about 1 ns, L2 about 4 ns, L3 about 15 ns and main memory about 80 ns, and current solid-state drives are faster than the listed figure. More importantly the ordering itself can invert: a fast local solid-state read against a slow cross-datacenter hop is no longer obviously the worse choice. So the method is to re-derive the hierarchy for the hardware in front of you and keep only the structural fact — each level down is orders of magnitude slower, and the count of crossings dominates whatever you do between them.

problem.practice: Take a slow query or endpoint you own and count crossings rather than operations: how many times does it reach main memory, storage, and another machine? Then check the arithmetic — if the work between the crossings is trivial, no algorithmic change will help you.

beats.broke: Storage was reasoned about as one thing called memory, so code was written as though reaching any of it cost the same — and the arithmetic units spent their time waiting.
beats.fix: Treat the hierarchy as a design input: each level is orders of magnitude slower than the one above, so the question for any hot operation is which level it touches and how often.
beats.cost: The ratios are durable and the absolute figures are not, so the table has to be re-derived for the hardware in front of you rather than quoted — and the ordering itself can invert.

interview.trap: Reciting the figures without the ratios, or quoting them as current. They come from a table dating to around 2012, and the point was never the values — it was that each level down is orders of magnitude slower than the one above.
interview.answer:
They matter as ratios rather than values, and the ratios are large enough to decide designs on their own.

From the table compiled by Jeff Dean, originally by Peter Norvig: an L1 reference is 0.5 ns, a branch mispredict 5 ns, an L2 reference 7 ns, a mutex lock and unlock 25 ns, and a main memory reference 100 ns — which the table labels 200x L1. That is why an index exists. Without one, a query reads the table, and a large table means many seeks of four human months each. An index makes the search structure shallow so the seek count collapses, which means the entire purpose of the data structure is reducing crossings into the slowest level.
